blocks.title: Ferrofluid
blocks.text: A ferrofluid is a unique material that exhibits both liquid and magnetic properties; it operates through a combination of magnetic and fluid dynamics principles. Essentially, a ferrofluid is a colloidal suspension of magnetic particles in a carrier fluid such as oil or water.

Typically the magnetic particles are iron oxide, ground to the nano-scale, approximately 10 nanometres in size. These particles are coated with a surfactant, a substance that reduces surface tension. This coating prevents the particles from clumping together, ensuring that they remain evenly dispersed in the fluid. The viscosity of the fluid, the nanometre size of the particles and their constant movement prevent the particles from settling down.

When there is no magnet around, a ferrofluid acts like a liquid; but when a magnet is nearby, the particles are temporarily magnetized and the fluid becomes a magnet. They form structures within the fluid, causing the ferrofluid to act more like a solid. When the magnet is removed, the particles are demagnetized and the ferrofluid acts like a liquid again. The first ferrofluid, developed by NASA in 1960, was ground from natural magnetite; it was invented to move liquids through space (For Your Information).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book dates the first ferrofluid to 1960. Ferrofluid was developed at NASA by Steve Papell in the early 1960s (his method was filed for a patent in 1963), so 1960 is too early.

This phenomenon is due to the competition between magnetic forces, surface tension and gravity. In the presence of a strong magnetic field, chain-like structures form because magnetic forces pull the fluid upward while gravity and surface tension pull it back down. These chains align along the magnetic field lines and increase the viscosity, making the fluid behave like a solid bulging in certain directions; these bulges are commonly known as spikes. The spikes form where the magnetic forces overcome the other forces (Fig. 10.17).

You need some laser printer toner, some cooking oil, a test tube, a glass bottle, a small stick and a magnet. Procedure: pour some toner into the test tube; laser printer toner contains 40% iron oxide in nanometre particle size. Add some cooking oil and mix it well with the stick to form a ferrofluid, and put this fluid in the bottle. The fluid acts like a liquid when the bottle is shaken. Now bring the magnet near the fluid outside the bottle: the fluid jumps towards the magnet, because it has itself become a magnet. If we hold the magnet on the side of the bottle, we see a structure with spikes formed by the fluid (Fig. 10.18).

items: Electronics: ferrofluids are used in rotary seals for computer hard drives and other rotating-shaft motors. In loudspeakers they cool the voice coil, which can heat up during operation: the magnetic field holds the fluid around the coil, allowing it to absorb and dissipate heat more effectively. They also damp vibrations in speakers and improve sound quality.

Medicine: ferrofluids can be directed to specific areas of the body using external magnets, allowing targeted drug delivery. The magnetic particles can carry drugs directly to a tumour or other target, reducing side effects and improving treatment efficiency. Ferrofluids can also be used as contrast agents in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Other applications include damping, or precisely controlling the flow of liquids by manipulating the magnetic field. Ferrofluids are used in electronics, medicine, engineering and active research in physics and materials science.
